title: How High Blood Pressure Quietly Raises Your Stroke Risk — and 8 Ways to Protect Your Brain
excerpt: Hypertension damages blood vessels in the brain long before symptoms appear. Neurologists say early intervention is one of the most effective defences against stroke and cognitive decline.
body:
• High blood pressure is the single most important modifiable risk factor for stroke, damaging blood vessels and promoting clots long before symptoms appear.
  • About 48% of American adults have high blood pressure, and South Asians face an elevated cardiovascular risk profile.
  • Research links uncontrolled mid-life hypertension to both stroke and later cognitive decline, including dementia.
  • Eight evidence-based lifestyle changes can significantly reduce risk, from the DASH diet to regular blood pressure monitoring at home.

High blood pressure sends roughly 400 to 500 patients a year to a single regional hospital for stroke treatment, according to Dr. Jack Rose, a neurointensivist at Washington Health. Across the United States, stroke is the fifth-leading cause of death. And the primary driver, neurologists say, is a condition that most people never feel: hypertension.

"Blood pressure is the most important factor contributing to brain injury, often in the form of a stroke," said Dr. Steven Greenberg, a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School. "Keeping blood pressure low can make brain injury less likely, help conserve brain function, and perhaps slow the natural decline in cognitive function."

The Silent Mechanism

A blood pressure reading above 130/80 mm Hg is considered elevated. At those levels, sustained pressure begins to damage the blood vessels that supply the brain. Over years, it helps clog arteries, weakens vessel walls, and promotes the formation of blood clots — creating the conditions for both ischemic strokes (caused by blockages) and hemorrhagic strokes (caused by ruptures).

Research from Boston University Medical School has shown that sustained hypertension can cause cerebral small vessel disease, a condition that narrows the brain's tiny arteries. This connects high blood pressure directly to both stroke and the development of dementia later in life.

"Controlling your blood pressure is one of the most effective ways to reduce your risk of stroke and dementia. There's really no reason for anyone to have high blood pressure that is uncontrolled."

— Dr. Deborah A. Levine, University of Michigan Medical School

A Particular Concern for South Asians

The stakes are especially high for people of South Asian descent, who face a disproportionately elevated risk of cardiovascular disease. Studies have consistently shown that Indians develop hypertension and heart disease at younger ages and at lower body weights than many other populations, making early screening and intervention critical — whether living in India or abroad.

8 Evidence-Based Ways to Protect Your Brain

1. Treat high blood pressure early. Work with a doctor to bring readings below 130/80. Medication, when prescribed, should be taken consistently.

2. Lower LDL cholesterol. "Bad" cholesterol narrows and clogs blood vessels in the brain. Statins and dietary changes both help.

3. Manage blood sugar. Diabetes damages blood vessels throughout the body, including in the brain. Keeping glucose under control reduces compounding risk.

4. Quit smoking. Cigarette smoke helps clog arteries, promotes blood clots, and damages the cells lining blood vessels.

5. Lose excess weight. Every two pounds lost translates to roughly a one-point drop in blood pressure, according to the Center for Science in the Public Interest.

6. Move more, sit less. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week — brisk walking counts — and avoid sitting for more than 11 hours a day.

7. Eat a DASH-style diet. Fill half the plate with fruits and vegetables. Add low-fat dairy, beans, nuts, fish, and poultry. Limit sodium, which is concentrated in processed foods, restaurant meals, and deli meats.

8. Monitor at home. A validated home blood pressure monitor, used twice daily for at least one week per month, provides data that office visits alone cannot capture. Morning and evening readings give a clearer picture of how pressure fluctuates.

What the research increasingly makes clear is that the window for intervention is in middle age — the 40s to early 60s — before damage accumulates. By the time symptoms of a stroke appear, the injury is already underway. The most effective protection is the least dramatic: checking a number, and acting on it early.
